title: Blues come into the street bands after a Zulu funeral
summary: Miller recalls that he, Black Benny, Henry Martin and others played blues up-tempo on the way back from a funeral, after which all the bands did; dated about 1923-24.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Did you see any changes in the brass bands from the time you got here to the time you left, say, 1919 to 1940?

Well, yeah, from what I can see, Tick, Black Benny, Lewis, and myself, and Henry Martin. Yeah. And some of them did change it while I was here. And after one big parade one day, we come back playing, you know, the blues stuff on the street. They didn't play blues on the street. Henry, and then Rosino decided to play some blues, play them fast, you know. Henry who? Henry Martin, I mean, not Henry Rosino. And we come back playing the blues in an up-tempo, you know, where you could walk right along with us, see. And boy, boy, boy. And after that, all the bands started playing blues on the street.
Yeah, I was working with them. Three chumpers, I was in there, Louie and me. Quite a prophet, actually. One of the Zulus had died, huh? One of the Zulus had died. Yeah.
I don't know his name, I didn't know his name. Well, what year would that be about?
It was before, though he left to join King Long.
So that was, and after you got.
How did you get here, about 26?
No, he left here about 22 to join Long. Yeah, he was four years. So, you got here in 1919. That's right. So we got it down to about three years, Sam.
